clinicalPearls: An anteriorly displaced and prominent Schwalbe line, seen as a fine white ring or arc just inside the limbus
It is a common, usually incidental finding that can occur in normal eyes
It is a hallmark feature of Axenfeld-Rieger spectrum when accompanied by iris strands and other anomalies
In isolation it is benign, but as part of anterior segment dysgenesis it carries a significant glaucoma risk
Gonioscopy demonstrates the prominent Schwalbe line and any attached iris processes
Identification should prompt assessment for associated iris changes, glaucoma and systemic features of Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome
reference.pathophysiology: Posterior embryotoxon represents an anteriorly positioned, thickened Schwalbe line, the peripheral termination of Descemet membrane at the angle. It arises from abnormal development of the neural crest-derived anterior segment tissues. When isolated it is a benign anatomical variant, but when it occurs with iridocorneal adhesions and iris hypoplasia it is part of the Axenfeld-Rieger spectrum of anterior segment dysgenesis, in which maldevelopment of the drainage angle predisposes to glaucoma.
additionalDifferentials: Arcus lipoides (which is stromal, not at Schwalbe line)
additionalInvestigations: Assessment of the iris for hypoplasia and corectopia
Intraocular pressure measurement and glaucoma evaluation
Systemic assessment for Axenfeld-Rieger features (dental, facial, umbilical) where relevant
redFlags: Associated iris anomalies indicating Axenfeld-Rieger spectrum
reference.prognosis: Isolated posterior embryotoxon is benign with no visual consequence; when part of anterior segment dysgenesis, prognosis depends on glaucoma control.
pitfalls: Dismissing it without checking for associated iris changes and glaucoma
Overlooking the systemic associations of Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome
Confusing it with arcus or other peripheral corneal findings
Failing to screen the family in syndromic cases
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Requires no ocular treatment when isolated, as it is a benign anatomical variant
Perform gonioscopy and slit-lamp examination to detect iris strands, corectopia and iris hypoplasia indicating the Axenfeld-Rieger spectrum
Measure intraocular pressure and undertake lifelong glaucoma surveillance where anterior segment dysgenesis is present
Treat associated glaucoma with topical pressure-lowering agents, escalating to angle or filtration surgery when medical control fails
Assess for systemic Axenfeld-Rieger features (dental, craniofacial and periumbilical anomalies) and refer accordingly
Offer genetic counselling and family examination given the autosomal dominant inheritance of the Axenfeld-Rieger spectrum
